headlines.title: He Left Uber to Fix Farming's Billion-Dollar Problem
headlines.summary: American farmers could spend $12 billion this year fighting weeds with chemical herbicides that can damage soil, threaten the environment, and put the people growing our food at risk. A Seattle startup thinks lasers are the fix.*Why do some startups take off and others don't? Get the answer:* https://clickhubspot.com/jm4eHerbicides took off in the 1940s, but weeds evolved to resist them, and in some cases that meant spraying more, with some farmers now applying glyphosate three to six times a season. Carbon Robotics’ LaserWeeder is built to break that cycle: cameras and an AI trained on more than 150 million plant images tell crop from weed, then a laser burns out the weed’s growth center in about 100 milliseconds, up to 10,000 times a minute. But one wrong shot could kill the crop next to it. And at around $800,000 a machine, it has to beat hand crews and herbicides on cost, not just on novelty. Noelle went to Salinas, California, to see how it holds up in the field, what farmers running it 22 hours a day are actually saving, and why a company with over $100 million in annual revenue still isn’t profitable.0:00 The LaserWeeder1:12 Inside the Machine’s AI Brain3:57 Why Traditional Weeding Fails5:29 The Hidden Costs of Herbicides6:39 From Uber to LaserWeeding8:05 Farmer Reactions to the New Tech9:59 The $800K Machine and the ROI13:35 Lasers vs. Hand Weeding15:36 Test Plots, Expansion, and Japan16:01 Autonomy, Scale, and ProfitabilityGet the 5-minute newsletter keeping 2M+ innovators in the loop: https://thehustle.

headlines.title: DoorDash Is Close to Buying Instacart for $17 Billion After Uber Walked Away

headlines.summary: The average brokerage recommendation (ABR) for Uber (UBER) is equivalent to a Buy. The overly optimistic recommendations of Wall Street analysts make the effectiveness of this highly sought-after metric questionable. So, is it worth buying the stock?

description: Uber Technologies, Inc. develops and operates proprietary technology applications in the United States, Canada, Latin America, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and the Asia Pacific. The company operates through three segments: Mobility, Delivery, and Freight. The Mobility segment connects consumers with a range of transportation modalities, such as ridesharing, carsharing, micromobility, rentals, public transit, taxis, and other modalities; and offers riders in a variety of vehicle types, as well as financial partnerships products and advertising services. The Delivery segment allows consumers to search for and discover restaurants to grocery, alcohol, convenience, and other retailers, as well as order a meal or other items, and either pick-up at the restaurant or have it delivered; and provides Uber direct, a white-label delivery-as-a-service for retailers and restaurants, as well as advertising services. The Freight segment manages transportation and logistics networks, which connects shippers and carriers in digital marketplace, including carriers upfronts, pricing, and shipment booking; and offers on-demand platform to automate logistics end-to-end transactions for small-and medium-sized businesses to global enterprises. Uber Technologies, Inc. has strategic partnership with Mews to embed ride booking, real-time tracking and integrated billing directly into the Mews platform. The company was formerly known as Ubercab, Inc. and changed its name to Uber Technologies, Inc. in February 2011. Uber Technologies, Inc. was founded in 2009 and is headquartered in San Francisco, California.
